97.3 What was checked, and what was not

Not verified in this revision: the current structure of the OMRH; the crop table in Part 95.2 (general knowledge); the number of public schools per commune and the thresholds in Part 96.3; the number of PE teachers today.

97.4 Open decisions added

  1. Targeted pools: the recommended version (a returned deposit, one pool at a time, no paid odds) or the author's proposal (a high fee for each move between pools, with a university degree or profession required).
  2. The absence limits and the size of the reserve list (Part 93).
  3. The length of training for each role within the 1-to-3-month range (Part 94).
  4. The thresholds for one, two or three sports complexes per commune (Part 96).
  5. Whether private schools must build their own grounds or may share public ones (Part 96).

t: PART 98 — MONEY THAT WORKS FOR HAITIANS: BANKS, SAVINGS, AND LOANS FOR FARMS AND SMALL BUSINESS
h:
PART 98 — MONEY THAT WORKS FOR HAITIANS: BANKS, SAVINGS, AND LOANS FOR FARMS AND SMALL BUSINESS

98.1 The problem in numbers

A World Bank study published in 2019 found that:

  • only about 0.8% of bank loans in Haiti went to agriculture, the country's largest employer;
  • only about 3% of rural adults had a formal loan, and only about 17% had an account at a financial institution;
  • farmers who borrow informally often pay 10–20% for one crop season, and some moneylenders charge more than 20% a month;
  • the main barriers are no accepted collateral, land without papers, no insurance against storms and drought, few roads and stores, and banks that see farming as too risky.

Haitians save and work hard. The money does not reach them. Deposits are lent to a few large firms and to the state, while the farmer, the madan sara and the young workshop owner go to the moneylender.

98.2 The goal

Within ten years: every adult has a free basic account; every farmer and small business can borrow at a fair, published price; no family loses its land or its harvest to a loan shark; and the financial system survives storms without collapsing.

98.3 A free account for every adult

  1. A basic account on the payment rail (Part 32), opened with the national ID card, free of monthly fees, usable by phone, with a debit card on request.
  2. Every public payment goes there: wages, pensions, family allowance, farm purchases, refunds.
  3. Agents in every communal section (shops, credit unions, post points) where cash can be put in and taken out.

98.4 The Haitian Development Bank

  1. One public development bank for farms, fishing, processing, small and medium business, housing and young entrepreneurs, built from the State's existing public financial institutions rather than a new one beside them.
  2. It mostly lends through others. It refinances credit unions, microfinance institutions and commercial banks that lend to farmers and small firms, so the loan officer stays close to the borrower.
  3. No political loans. Credit decisions are made by trained loan officers under published rules. A loan to a minister, an Assembly member, a judge, their families or their companies is published by name and approved by the board's audit committee (Part 39).
  4. A cross-selected board (central bank, farmers' and business organizations, credit unions, independent experts, citizens drawn by lot), and annual accounts audited and published.
  5. Results on the ledger: loans by commune, sector, gender and size; default rates; cost per loan.

98.5 Making loans possible without land papers

  1. A guarantee fund (Part 59.1) that pays part of the loss if a farm or small-business loan fails, for example half. The lender always keeps part of the risk, so it still checks carefully.
  2. New things can serve as collateral: animals, tools, motorbikes, a purchase contract with the State Export Board (Part 51.2), and warehouse receipts: a farmer stores rice, coffee or cocoa at the commune packing house (Part 95.4), receives a receipt, and borrows against it instead of selling at harvest when prices are lowest.
  3. A public register of movable collateral, online, so that a lender can see if an animal or a machine is already pledged.
  4. Group loans through cooperatives and farmers' groups, where members guarantee each other.
  5. The land cadastre (Part 20) will later let land serve as collateral, with a rule that a family's home and last plot cannot be seized for a small loan.

98.6 Insurance against storms and drought

  • Farm insurance by index: when rain, wind or an earthquake passes a measured level in a zone, every insured farmer there is paid automatically, without an inspector visiting each field.
  • The State pays part of the premium for small farmers in the first years.
  • Haiti also uses regional disaster insurance for the State itself, so that public money arrives quickly after a hurricane.

98.7 Fair lending rules

  1. One price, in Kreyòl. Every loan shows the total yearly cost, all fees included, in one number, on one page, in Kreyòl. Hidden fees are void.
  2. Average interest rates by type of lender are published each quarter, so borrowers can compare.
  3. Licences for moneylenders. Anyone who lends for profit as a business registers. Threats, violence, seizing a child's papers, or taking land without a court order are crimes.
  4. A free complaint and mediation service at the central bank for bank and loan disputes.
  5. A credit history for the poor. The central bank's credit information office includes credit unions, microfinance, and on-time payment of phone and electricity bills, so that a person without a bank loan can still prove they pay.
  6. Deposit insurance: small savers' deposits are protected by a fund paid for by the banks.

98.8 Banks that lend in Haiti

  • The central bank continues and strengthens its incentives (lower reserve requirements) for banks that lend to agriculture and small business.
  • Each bank publishes each quarter how much of its deposits it lends to the private sector in Haiti, by sector and département.
  • New banks and credit unions may enter under strict prudential rules, so that a few institutions do not decide for the whole country.
  • Credit unions and microfinance are regulated by a modern law and supervised by risk, so that savers are safe.

98.9 Traditional savings: the sòl

The sòl (rotating savings group) has financed Haitian families for generations.

  • It is recognized and left free. No licence is needed for a sòl among people who know each other.
  • Digital sòl apps may be offered by private companies, cooperatives and banks, licensed by the central bank and connected to the payment rail. The licence requires: 1. Members' money kept in a protected trust account at a bank, never mixed with the company's own money and never lent out. 2. Identity checks for every member (Part 54). 3. The order of turns, every payment and every payout visible to all members of the group. 4. All fees shown before joining, in Kreyòl. 5. Protection against a member who receives the pot and stops paying: a deposit, insurance, or turns ordered by payment record. 6. Members' data protected (Part 6) and never sold.
  • A sòl group that saves regularly can use its record to get a group loan (98.5).

98.10 The diaspora as investor

  • Diaspora accounts and bonds for projects that earn (power, irrigation, housing), never for salaries (Part 59.3).
  • A remittance can become a mortgage: a family that receives regular transfers can use that record to borrow for a house built to the safety standard (Part 64).

98.11 Learning about money

Money lessons in every school from the age of 10: saving, interest, budgets, the sòl, how to read a loan, and how to recognize a fraud. Free short courses for farmers and traders at every Sovereign House.

98.12 Capture test and honest limits

Risk What stops it
The development bank becomes a piggy bank for friends Published loans to covered persons; cross-selected board; audits
The guarantee fund pays for bad loans Lenders keep part of the loss; payout rates published by lender
Insurance is captured by insurers Public tender; payout rules published before the season
  • A development bank can lose a lot of money. Several countries' farm banks failed through political loans and forgiven debts. This bank lends mostly through others, keeps lenders at risk, and forbids mass debt forgiveness except after a declared disaster with a published rule.
  • Fair-price rules can push some lenders out of the market. That is why the rule is transparency and licensing, not a hard cap that drives lending underground.
  • None of this works while armed groups control roads. Security comes first (Part 59.1).

t: PART 99 — A KONBIT NATION: FAMILY, NEIGHBOURS, AND LIFE BEYOND THE CROWDED CITY
h:
PART 99 — A KONBIT NATION: FAMILY, NEIGHBOURS, AND LIFE BEYOND THE CROWDED CITY

99.1 What Haiti had, and must keep

In Haiti, when someone died, the neighbours came: they cooked, sat up through the night, carried the coffin and gave what they could. When a child was born, the women of the lakou came to help. When a field had to be cleared, the konbit gathered, worked together with songs, and ate together. This is the strongest social security Haiti ever had, and it cost the State nothing. Crowded cities, violence and migration have broken much of it. This Part protects and rebuilds it.

99.2 The principle

The State supports families and communities. It does not replace them, and it does not order them. Help is offered, never imposed (Part 57.1).

99.3 Konbit recognized and supported

  1. Konbit Days: each communal section may hold community work days (roads, drains, cleaning, tree planting, school repair). The commune supplies tools, materials, water and a meal; the Section Coordinator (Part 81) records the work.
  2. Konbit for the needy: a family whose house was damaged, or a widow who cannot work her field, may ask the section for a konbit.
  3. Participation is free and voluntary. Nobody is forced, paid in votes, or punished for not coming.
  4. Konbit work counts toward young people's civic service (Part 38.4).

99.4 Birth and death: no family alone

  1. Every birth: a visit by a community health agent in the first week (Part 36), a baby kit, and birth registration at home.
  2. Every death of a poor person: a burial allowance paid on the payment rail within 48 hours, a dignified place in a maintained public cemetery, and help with the death certificate.
  3. Mutual aid societies (sosyete, funeral and burial societies, church groups) are recognized by a simple registration, protected from fraud, and may receive a small public matching contribution when their accounts are clear.

99.5 The lakou in housing

  • The housing program (Part 34) and the land rules (Part 20) allow family compounds: several houses of one family around a shared yard, on one plot, built to the safety standard (Part 64).
  • New neighbourhoods are designed around shared courtyards, small squares, a market, a school and a sports ground (Part 96), not endless rows of walls.
  • Elders stay with the family (Part 57.2): a caregiver allowance, home visits, and day centres in every commune where grandparents meet.

99.6 Neighbours settle small quarrels

  • A community mediation desk in every communal section for small disputes (boundaries, animals, noise, small debts, family quarrels), run by trained mediators chosen by the community, with the agreement written down.
  • Mediation is free and voluntary. It never handles violent crimes, sexual abuse or abuse of children, which go to the police and courts. Anyone can go to court instead.

99.7 Life beyond the crowded city

Port-au-Prince grew without a plan because jobs, schools, hospitals and offices were all there. To make life good in every département:

  1. Services follow people: a hospital in every département capital, a clinic within 30 minutes (Part 5.5), secondary schools in every commune, university campuses spread across the country (Part 73).
  2. The State leaves the capital: national agencies are based in different départements — for example farm agencies in the Artibonite, fisheries in the South, border agencies near the Gates. Fewer people must move to the capital to work for the State or to deal with it.
  3. Jobs where the land is: processing plants, packing houses and cold rooms in the communes (Parts 51, 95), so food is processed where it grows.
  4. Power and internet in every section (Part 5.3), so a young person can work for a company abroad from a village.
  5. Towns of the right size: the commune plan (Part 65) keeps towns low and green, with markets, squares and gardens.
  6. No one is forced to move. People choose. The State makes the choice to stay or to return home a real one (Part 52).

99.8 Capture test and honest limits

  • A konbit can be turned into forced labour by a local boss, or into a vote-buying event by a party. It is voluntary, records are public, and party symbols are forbidden at it (Part 92).
  • Mutual aid societies handle money; fraud happens. Clear accounts are the condition for public support.
  • Moving agencies out of the capital costs money and can disrupt service. It happens office by office, with a published plan.

t: PART 100 — PROTECTING CHILDREN AND HAITIAN CULTURE: PROMOTE FIRST, LIMIT WHAT HARMS, BAN ONLY BY A JUDGE
h:
PART 100 — PROTECTING CHILDREN AND HAITIAN CULTURE: PROMOTE FIRST, LIMIT WHAT HARMS, BAN ONLY BY A JUDGE

100.1 The concern

Many Haitians worry that imported culture is replacing their own: violent music and films, songs that celebrate armed groups, and a loss of respect. Armed groups use social media, music videos and songs to recruit children, threaten people and celebrate killings. Children must be protected, and Haitian culture must be strong.

100.2 The choice this Part makes

A board that bans music, films or tattoos is a dangerous tool. Whoever controls it decides what Haitians may hear and see, and it can be used to silence protest songs and critics, as dictatorships have done in Haiti and elsewhere. The capture test asks: "If the wrong people controlled this board, what would they ban?" The answer is: songs against them.

So this Part does three things:

  1. Promote Haitian culture strongly, so that it wins by quality and presence.
  2. Protect children with clear rules on age, time and place.
  3. Ban only what causes direct harm (recruiting for armed groups, threats, celebrating real crimes, sexual content involving children), and only by a judge's order.

100.3 Promote Haitian culture

  • Haitian music on Haitian airwaves: radio stations broadcast at least half Haitian music (made in Haiti or by the diaspora), and television stations at least 40% Haitian programs, reached over five years.
  • Funding: the Storytelling Fund (Part 40.8) supports Haitian films, series, music, children's programs and video games, in Kreyòl first.
  • Music in every school (Part 72): konpa, rara, twoubadou, mizik rasin, classical and church music, with instruments.
  • Festivals and national days (Part 57.4) funded in every département; carnival and rara safe and supported.
  • Kreyòl online: Haitian content on platforms, children's cartoons in Kreyòl, and support for Haitian creators.

100.4 Protect children

  1. Age ratings for films, series, video games and music videos, by an independent rating board (parents, teachers, artists, child psychologists, citizens drawn by lot). Ratings inform parents; they do not ban.
  2. Time rules: television and radio do not broadcast violent or sexual content before 10 p.m.
  3. Place rules: no violent or sexual content in schools, children's spaces, public buses or public screens. Cinemas check age for adult films.
  4. Online: platforms operating in Haiti offer parental controls in Kreyòl and act quickly on court orders (100.5).
  5. Advertising: no advertising of alcohol, tobacco or gambling aimed at children, or near schools.
  6. No tattoos on children: tattooing a person under 18 is forbidden.
  7. Parents first: free guidance for parents on screens, games and online risks.

100.5 What is banned, and how

These are crimes, decided by a judge, not by a ministry:

  • Content made or paid for by armed groups to recruit, threaten, extort or celebrate real killings, kidnappings or rapes.
  • Direct threats and incitement to violence against identified people or groups (Part 6; Part 63 for racism).
  • Sexual content involving children, in any form.

A judge can order the removal of such content and the closing of an account. Every order is published with its reason and can be appealed. No minister, police chief or board can ban a song, a film or a book by decision.

100.6 Tattoos and personal style

  • Adults decide for themselves. Tattoos, hair and dress are private choices (Part 57.6).
  • Uniformed services (police, army, customs, Coast Guard) may set rules on visible tattoos while in uniform, like many armies and police forces.
  • Gang marks: a tattoo is never a crime and never proof of a crime on its own.

100.7 Honest limits

  • Most young people get their music and films on phones from abroad. Quotas on Haitian radio and television help, but the real answer is Haitian content good enough to compete.
  • "Violent music" means different things to different people. A rule built on taste would be applied unequally and could target poor neighbourhoods. That is why this Part bans conduct (recruiting, threats, celebrating real crimes), not styles.
  • Open decision: the author's proposal to go further and restrict tattoos and violent music and films by law is recorded in Part 102.

t: PART 101 — DRUGS: STRICT LIKE JAPAN, WITH TREATMENT FOR THE ADDICTED AND NO WELCOME FOR FOREIGN USERS
h:
PART 101 — DRUGS: STRICT LIKE JAPAN, WITH TREATMENT FOR THE ADDICTED AND NO WELCOME FOR FOREIGN USERS

101.1 Why this matters now

Haiti has become a major transit point for drugs moving from South America toward the United States and the Caribbean. The United Nations has warned that armed groups controlling key corridors are linked to international trafficking networks. In July 2025, Haitian authorities seized 1,045 kg of cocaine near Tortuga, the largest seizure in more than 30 years. Drug money buys guns, police, judges and votes. A country that wants to be the safest on earth (Part 68) must shut this door.

101.2 The model

Japan has very low drug use and very strict laws: possession and use of drugs are crimes, cannabis use was made a separate crime in December 2024, and foreigners convicted of drug offences are deported and refused entry. Haiti adopts the same firmness, inside its own Constitution, which abolished the death penalty (1987, Art. 20).

101.3 The rules

  1. No legal recreational drugs. Cannabis, cocaine, crack, heroin, methamphetamine, synthetic drugs and their analogues are illegal to grow, make, import, sell, carry or use. A published list is updated by the Ministry of Health with the drug control commission.
  2. Medicines that can be abused (strong painkillers, sedatives, stimulants) are sold only by pharmacies, on a registered prescription, with every sale recorded.
  3. Alcohol and tobacco remain legal for adults 18 and over, with no sale to minors, no sale near schools, and no advertising aimed at the young. Traditional drinks such as kleren are made under the Food Standard (Part 50).

101.4 Penalties (ranges for the drafting body to set exactly)

Offence Penalty
Trafficking, importing, making, or selling Long prison sentences, heavier for large amounts, for selling to children, near schools, or by a public official; all assets from the trade confiscated (Part 46)
Financing or protecting traffickers (officials, police, soldiers, judges, customs) The heaviest sentences in this Part, removal from office, loss of pension rights earned during the crime
Possession or use, first time Criminal conviction, with a choice: supervised treatment and testing for 6–12 months, or prison. Success leads to a suspended sentence
Possession or use, repeated Prison, with treatment inside (Part 42)
Driving, piloting, or carrying a weapon under drugs Prison and loss of the licence

101.5 Foreigners

  • A foreigner convicted of a drug offence serves the sentence in full.
  • The court also orders the person to pay the costs of the arrest, the trial, the administrative fees and the deportation, according to a published schedule of costs.
  • These costs are taken first from money and goods seized and from any bail.
  • A person who can pay and refuses stays in custody after the sentence until the costs are paid, up to a maximum set by law. A person who truly cannot pay is deported at the end of the sentence, because keeping them in prison would cost Haiti more; the debt stays on record and the person's country is asked to pay for the travel.
  • After deportation, the person is banned from entering Haiti for five years, and in any case until the costs are paid. A second drug offence brings a life ban.
  • A foreigner with a drug conviction anywhere may be refused a visa or entry.
  • Diplomatic immunity is respected, but the person is declared unwelcome (persona non grata) and the case is made public.
  • Haitian citizens are never deported. They receive the same sentences and the same order to pay the costs, by instalments on the payment rail (Part 32). A citizen who can pay and refuses faces the same limited extra custody.

101.6 Testing

Random drug tests for police, soldiers, Coast Guard, customs officers, judges, prison staff, pilots, bus and truck drivers, and anyone who carries a licensed firearm (Part 61). A positive test means removal from duty, a second test, and discipline. Tests are done by accredited laboratories, with a right to a second sample.

101.7 Closing the routes

  • Sea, air and land watch (Parts 49, 90): radar, Coast Guard, registered wharves, scanned containers, the Line watched 24 hours.
  • Every airstrip registered; an unregistered landing strip is destroyed.
  • Follow the money: the financial intelligence unit (UCREF) and the ledger (Part 8) trace drug money; banks report suspicious transactions (Part 98).
  • Regional cooperation with Caribbean and American partners on intelligence and extradition, under Haitian command (Part 44).

101.8 Prevention and treatment

  • Prevention in every school from age 10, sport and music as the alternative (Parts 72, 96).
  • A treatment centre in every département and outpatient care in every commune, free under the health insurance (Part 31).
  • Families are helped, not shamed: counselling and support groups.
  • Young people used by armed groups to carry or sell drugs follow the second-chance path of Part 76 if they committed no grave crime.

101.9 Capture test and honest limits

  • Drug laws can become a tool to target the poor while the big traffickers buy their freedom. Prosecution numbers are published by amount seized and by level (street seller, transporter, organizer, financier); a system that jails only street sellers is failing.
  • Planting drugs on someone is a serious crime. Every search is filmed (Part 62), and seized drugs are weighed and sealed in front of a witness.
  • Strict laws do not work alone. Japan's low drug use also comes from culture, family and strong policing; Haiti must build those too.
  • Treatment costs money, but prison costs more.

t: PART 102 — RECORD OF THIS REVISION (PARTS 98–101)
h:
PART 102 — RECORD OF THIS REVISION (PARTS 98–101)

102.1 What changed

Older text Change
Parts 32 and 59.1: the payment rail and the guarantee fund A free account for every adult; a development bank; new collateral; farm insurance; fair lending rules; the sòl (Part 98)
Part 57: family and tradition Konbit, help at birth and death, the lakou, community mediation, life beyond the crowded city (Part 99)
Parts 6 and 40.8: media and storytelling Haitian content quotas, child protection by age, time and place, bans only by a judge (Part 100)
No earlier Part on drugs Strict drug law, treatment, deportation and life ban for foreign offenders, testing, closing the routes (Part 101)

102.2 What was checked, and what was not

Checked: the World Bank's 2019 study of farm finance in Haiti; the United Nations warning and the July 2025 seizure near Tortuga (press report); the December 2024 change to Japan's cannabis law (press report).

Not verified: the exact penalties in Japanese law and the length of Japan's entry ban; Haiti's current drug law and the work of its drug control commission; current loan and account figures (the 2019 numbers may have changed); the current deposit insurance and credit information rules of the central bank.

102.3 Open decisions added

  1. Culture: the approach of Part 100 (promote, protect children, ban only by a judge), or the author's proposal to restrict tattoos and violent music and films by law.
  2. The exact drug penalties and the length of supervised treatment (Part 101).
  3. The radio and television quotas for Haitian content (Part 100).
  4. Which public institutions form the development bank (Part 98).
  5. Which national agencies move to which départements (Part 99).

t: PART 103 — TAXES PEOPLE ARE WILLING TO PAY: LIGHT, SIMPLE, FAIR, VISIBLE, AND A RESERVE FOR BAD DAYS
h:
PART 103 — TAXES PEOPLE ARE WILLING TO PAY: LIGHT, SIMPLE, FAIR, VISIBLE, AND A RESERVE FOR BAD DAYS

103.1 Where Haiti stands

  • Haiti collects very little tax: about 5–6% of the national economy (GDP), one of the lowest levels in the world (World Bank figures reported for 2023 and 2024).
  • The average for Latin America and the Caribbean is about 21%, and the average of rich OECD countries about 34% (2023). The United Kingdom is above 30%.
  • At the same time, people who do pay feel taxed too much: many import charges stack on top of each other, while large exemptions and smuggling let others pay nothing.

The problem is not that taxes are too low or too high. It is that too few pay, the rules are complicated, and nobody sees where the money goes.

103.2 The goal

  1. Enough to run the country and save for emergencies: raise total tax revenue step by step to about 15% of GDP within ten years.
  2. Never heavy: total taxes do not exceed 20% of GDP unless two-thirds of the Citizens' Assembly vote for it, for a limited time. Haiti stays lighter than the United Kingdom and below the Latin American average.
  3. Raise money by collecting from everyone, not by raising rates. Most of the increase comes from customs and taxes already owed and not collected, from ending exemptions for the connected, and from simple regimes that bring small businesses in.

103.3 Six principles

  1. Few taxes. A handful of clear taxes instead of dozens of small fees.
  2. Low rates, wide base. Everyone pays a little; nobody pays a lot.
  3. The poor pay no income tax. Income up to the living wage (Part 107) is tax-free.
  4. No favours. No exemption without a law, a published cost, a named beneficiary for large ones, and an end date.
  5. Pay by phone, in minutes. No queue, no cash to an officer.
  6. See where your money goes. Every gourde is on the ledger (Part 8).

103.4 The taxes

Tax Who pays Proposed rule
Income tax People with income above the living wage Tax-free up to the living wage; then 10%, 15%, 20%, and 25% at the top (Haiti's current top rate is 30%). Thresholds rise with prices every year. Employers withhold it from wages
Company tax Companies on their profit 25% (today 30%), with an allowance for companies that share profits with workers (Part 107)
Small business tax Traders, workshops and small firms below a published turnover One small monthly payment by phone, a low share of turnover, replacing income tax, company tax and TCA. No accountant needed
TCA (sales tax) Buyers, collected by registered businesses Stays at 10%. Zero on basic local food, medicines, school books and farm inputs. Small sellers below the threshold do not charge it
Property tax Owners of buildings and land Paid to the commune; see 103.5
Excise Buyers of alcohol, tobacco, sugary drinks, luxury cars Moderate rates, partly earmarked for health (Part 31)
Customs Importers Published values, one window, receipts (Parts 45, 49); stacked charges merged into one clear duty
Social contributions Employers and workers Pension and health insurance (Parts 23, 31), collected with income tax in one payment

Fuel: taxed lightly and steadily. Any change is announced in advance and phased in, never overnight.

Remittances: no new tax on money sent home. The existing levy is decided only after the audit of Part 84.

103.5 Property tax that stays in the commune

  • Based on the cadastre (Part 20): each property has a published value that the owner can contest.
  • Low rate. A modest family home is exempt.
  • Higher on land kept empty in towns and on large unused estates, so that land is built on or farmed instead of held for speculation.
  • Higher on second homes and luxury property.
  • All of it stays in the commune and is spent on local services. The commune publishes what it collected and how it was spent.
  • Pay early, pay less: a small discount for paying on time.

103.6 How taxes are collected

  1. One number: the national ID number (Part 54) is the tax number.
  2. Pre-filled returns: the tax office fills in what it already knows (wages, bank interest, property). The person checks and confirms by phone.
  3. Payment by phone on the payment rail (Part 32), with an instant receipt.
  4. No cash to any tax officer, ever. An officer who accepts cash is dismissed.
  5. Audits by rule: some files are chosen at random and some by published risk signs, never by an officer's choice. Inspectors rotate.
  6. Rights: a written reason for every assessment; a free tax ombudsman; appeal to the administrative court; no seizure of a family home for a small debt.
  7. A one-time fresh start: a short period to declare and pay past taxes without penalties, then firm enforcement.
  8. Big payers first: the largest companies and the richest people are checked first and most often, with their tax paid published in totals by sector.

103.7 Why people will be willing to pay

  • The receipt shows the use. Every tax receipt shows how each 100 gourdes of public money was spent last year: schools, health, police, roads, the reserve.
  • Local money, local choice. Citizens of each commune vote each year on how to spend part of the local budget (participatory budgeting).
  • Visible results. Tax revenue and spending by commune are on the ledger; a citizen can see the road or the clinic that their taxes built.
  • Fairness. No one escapes: the list of all tax exemptions, their cost and the large beneficiaries is published every year.
  • Respect. Clear rules, fast service and no bribes (Part 92).

103.8 The National Reserve Fund: money for bad days

Hurricanes, earthquakes, epidemics and price shocks will come. Haiti saves for them in good years.

  1. Each year, at least 3% of tax revenue goes into the National Reserve Fund, plus half of any unexpected windfall revenue.
  2. Target: the fund reaches the cost of three months of state spending, then is kept at that level.
  3. Safe: managed by the central bank under published rules, in safe assets, never lent to the government for ordinary spending.
  4. Only for real emergencies: money is released only after a declared disaster or emergency (Part 21), by a public vote of the Assembly, with every payment on the ledger.
  5. Refilled after use, on a published schedule.
  6. Together with insurance: regional disaster insurance (Part 98.6) pays fast after a storm; the reserve pays the rest.

103.9 Capture test and honest limits

Risk What stops it
Exemptions for friends Law, cost, beneficiary and end date published; the fiscal council reports on them (Part 59.3)
Officers take bribes No cash; random and rule-based audits; rotation
The reserve is raided Release only after a declared emergency and a public Assembly vote
  • The rates above are proposals. The independent fiscal council (Part 59.3) must model them before any law.
  • Most economic activity in Haiti is informal. The small-business tax and phone payment aim to bring it in gently; it will take years.
  • Lower rates can reduce revenue at first if collection does not improve quickly.

t: PART 104 — EVERY HAITIAN COUNTS: THE RIGHTS OF PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES
h:
PART 104 — EVERY HAITIAN COUNTS: THE RIGHTS OF PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES

104.1 Where Haiti stands

Haiti has ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Its law of 13 March 2012 forbids discrimination, calls for access to buildings, transport and information, and requires private employers with more than 20 workers to reserve 2% of jobs for people with disabilities. The State has a Secretary of State for the integration of persons with disabilities (BSEIPH). The 2010 earthquake left many thousands more Haitians with disabilities. The law exists. It is not applied.

104.2 The principle

A disability is a difference, not a curse, and not a reason to be left out. People with disabilities have the same rights as everyone, and the duty of the State and society is to remove the barriers.

104.3 Rights made real

  1. Education: every school accepts children with disabilities, with support (ramps, adapted material, trained teachers, assistants). Special classes only when the family chooses them.
  2. Haitian Sign Language is an official language of instruction for deaf children, taught to teachers and families, with interpreters in courts, hospitals, public offices and on national television news.
  3. Braille and audio for public documents, ballots, schoolbooks, and the Service Charter (Part 92).
  4. Accessible buildings: every new public building and every building open to the public meets the access standard (Part 64): ramps, wide doors, accessible toilets. Existing public buildings are adapted within ten years, schools and clinics first.
  5. Transport: new buses and stations are accessible; reserved seats; drivers trained.
  6. Health and devices: wheelchairs, prostheses, hearing aids, glasses and therapy are covered by health insurance (Part 31). A rehabilitation centre in every département.
  7. Early help: disabilities are detected early during the first-week visit and child health checks (Parts 36, 99.4), and families get support from the start.
  8. Work: the 2% quota is enforced in private firms; the public service reserves 4% of posts; an adaptation fund pays for workplace changes. Employers who do not meet the quota pay into that fund.
  9. Income: a disability allowance for those who cannot work, and a caregiver allowance for families who care for a person with a severe disability.
  10. Voting and public life: accessible polling places, help to vote in secret, and people with disabilities eligible for every pool and post (Part 91), with reasonable adjustments.
  11. Protection: abuse, abandonment or exploitation of a person with a disability is an aggravated crime. Living with family and community comes before any institution.
  12. In disasters: emergency plans list and help people with disabilities first (Part 21).

104.4 Who makes it happen

  • An independent Disability Rights Office that receives complaints, inspects, and can fine. Its board includes organizations of people with disabilities.
  • Counted: the census and surveys use standard questions on disability, and results are published by commune.
  • Nothing about us without us: organizations of people with disabilities sit on the boards of education, health, transport and building standards.
  • Changing minds: public campaigns, in Kreyòl, against the belief that disability is a punishment or a curse.

104.5 Honest limits

  • Adapting buildings and training teachers costs money and time. The plan starts with schools, clinics and public offices.
  • A quota without inspection is a promise on paper. Inspections and published results are the test.

t: PART 105 — MENTAL HEALTH: CARE NEAR HOME, IN KREYÒL, WITH THE FAMILY AND THE COMMUNITY
h:
PART 105 — MENTAL HEALTH: CARE NEAR HOME, IN KREYÒL, WITH THE FAMILY AND THE COMMUNITY

105.1 Where Haiti stands

In 2011, Haiti was reported to have fewer than 20 psychiatrists for more than 10 million people. Since then, earthquakes, hurricanes, kidnappings, armed-group violence and displacement have left very many Haitians with trauma, grief, depression and anxiety. Many people with mental illness are hidden at home, chained, or left on the street. A country cannot heal while its people carry wounds nobody treats.

105.2 The principle

Mental health is health. Care is offered near home, in Kreyòl, with respect, with the family, and without shame. It builds on what Haiti already has: the family, the lakou, the church and the community (Part 99).

105.3 Care in layers

Level Who What
Section Community health agents and trained volunteers Listening, psychological first aid, spotting serious illness, home visits, referral
Commune clinic A nurse or doctor trained in mental health, and a psychologist Treatment of common problems (depression, anxiety, trauma, alcohol and drugs), medicines, counselling
Département hospital A psychiatric unit inside the general hospital Short stays for serious illness, emergencies, specialist care
National Modernized public psychiatric hospitals and a training centre The most serious cases, training, research

The world's health agencies have shown that general nurses and doctors can treat the most common mental illnesses with short training. Haiti uses that approach first, because it cannot wait for hundreds of psychiatrists.

105.4 For the people who need it most

  • Victims of violence, kidnapping and rape: trauma care, free, confidential, and linked to the courts only if the victim chooses (Parts 41, 77).
  • Children: a trained counsellor for every group of schools; play and sport as care (Part 96); help for children who saw violence.
  • Young people leaving armed groups (Part 76) and people in prison (Part 42): treatment as part of their path back.
  • People who use drugs or alcohol: treatment centres (Part 101.8).
  • Mothers: care for depression during and after pregnancy.
  • The elderly: care for dementia, with support for the family.
  • Public workers under heavy stress: police, soldiers, nurses, teachers, members of the Assembly (Part 93): confidential support and rest.

105.5 A free line, day and night

A free, 24-hour help line in Kreyòl by phone and message, with trained listeners and a link to emergency help.

105.6 Preventing suicide

A national prevention plan: the help line, follow-up care for anyone who has attempted it, training for health workers, teachers and pastors to recognize the danger, responsible reporting rules for the media, and control of the means most often used.

105.7 Rights and dignity

  1. No chains, no cages, no beating, at home, in a hospital, a church, a temple or a prison. Families who do this out of fear get help, not punishment, the first time.
  2. Treatment without consent only when a person is a danger to themselves or others, decided by two doctors, reviewed by a judge within 72 hours, and limited in time.
  3. Equal cover: mental health care is covered by health insurance (Part 31) on the same terms as physical care.
  4. No discrimination at work, in school or in housing because of a mental illness.

105.8 Working with faith and tradition

Many Haitians first go to a pastor, a priest or a houngan when they suffer. The mental health service works with them with respect: training in recognizing serious illness, a referral path, and a shared rule — no harm, no chains, no abandonment. People keep their faith and also receive care.

105.9 Training the people

  • Funded training (Part 17.2) for psychologists, psychiatric nurses, social workers and psychiatrists, with service in the départements afterward.
  • Mental health in the training of every doctor, nurse, teacher and police officer.
  • Peer support groups in every commune: people who have recovered help others, in the konbit spirit.

105.10 Honest limits

  • Specialists will be few for many years. Training general health workers is the fastest path.
  • Stigma changes slowly. Public campaigns with known Haitian figures help.
  • Trauma will keep coming while violence continues. Security (Parts 41, 68) is also mental health.

t: PART 106 — THE CONSUMER IS PROTECTED: HONEST PRICES, REAL PRODUCTS, REFUNDS, AND NO POISON IN CREAMS OR HAIR PRODUCTS
h:
PART 106 — THE CONSUMER IS PROTECTED: HONEST PRICES, REAL PRODUCTS, REFUNDS, AND NO POISON IN CREAMS OR HAIR PRODUCTS

106.1 The problem

Haitians pay for fake medicines, expired food, products that break in a week with no refund, scales that cheat, and creams that damage the skin and the kidneys. Skin-lightening products sold in markets can contain mercury, strong steroid medicines and hydroquinone without any warning. The buyer has no one to turn to.

106.2 The Consumer Protection Agency

An independent agency with inspectors in every département, a free phone line, power to test, seize, fine and recall, and a board that includes consumer associations. It works with the Food Standard laboratory (Part 50) and customs at the Gates and ports (Parts 45, 49).

106.3 The buyer's rights

  1. Clear prices in gourdes, displayed before purchase, including all taxes.
  2. Honest weights and measures, checked in markets and shops (Part 90.2).
  3. Labels in Kreyòl or French: what it is, what it contains, who made it, the expiry date, how to use it safely.
  4. Refund, repair or replacement for a product that is defective or not as described: within 30 days for all goods, and within a one-year warranty for appliances, phones, vehicles and building materials.
  5. No sale of expired food or medicine. Expired goods are seized and destroyed.
  6. Fake goods: counterfeit medicines are a serious crime (Part 50); counterfeit goods are seized and destroyed, and importers are prosecuted.
  7. Fast justice: a small-claims procedure decided within 30 days, without a lawyer.
  8. Recalls: a dangerous product is recalled publicly, by radio and text message.
  9. Online and phone sales: the same rights, plus a 7-day right to cancel.

106.4 Fair prices without shortages

General price controls cause empty shelves and black markets. Fair prices come instead from competition (a competition authority that breaks up cartels and monopolies), published market prices of staples every day (Part 95.4), local production (Part 51), and honest customs (Part 45). In a declared emergency (Part 21), raising the price of essentials (water, food, fuel, medicine, building materials) far above normal is forbidden for a limited time.

106.5 Safe skin and hair products: what is banned and why

Product or ingredient Rule Why (the science)
Mercury in any cosmetic, cream or soap Banned Mercury passes through the skin and damages the kidneys and the nerves, and harms unborn children. The Minamata Convention on Mercury requires its parties to stop the making, import and sale of mercury-added cosmetics
Hydroquinone in cosmetics Banned in cosmetics; allowed only as a medicine on a doctor's prescription Long use can cause permanent dark-blue patches on the skin (ochronosis) and irritation. The European Union does not allow it in skin cosmetics
Strong steroid creams (such as clobetasol) sold as lighteners Prescription only Without medical control they thin the skin, cause infections, stretch marks and acne, and can disturb the body's hormones
Lead, arsenic and other heavy metals in cosmetics and hair dyes Banned above trace levels Toxic to the brain and organs, especially in children
Formaldehyde and formaldehyde-releasing ingredients in hair straighteners and "keratin" treatments Banned Formaldehyde is classified as a cause of cancer in humans; it irritates the eyes and lungs of users and hairdressers. The US food and drug agency has proposed banning it in hair-smoothing products
Chemical hair relaxers and straighteners Strict labeling and warnings; not sold for use on children A large US National Institutes of Health study (2022) found more uterine cancer among women who used hair straighteners often. The link is being studied further; until then, warnings and protection of children are the prudent rule

How it is enforced:

  • Every cosmetic and hair product sold in Haiti is registered, with its full ingredient list in Kreyòl or French.
  • Imports are tested at the Gates and ports; market samples are tested every month.
  • Sellers of banned products are fined and their stock destroyed; importers and makers are prosecuted.
  • Hairdressers and beauticians are trained in safe products and good ventilation.

106.6 Beauty without harm

The demand for lighter skin comes from the color prejudice that Part 63 makes illegal in hiring, schools and advertising. The agency and the Ministry of Health run campaigns that celebrate Haitian beauty in every shade, and advertising for skin lightening is banned.

106.7 Honest limits

  • Banned products will still be smuggled. Testing at the Gates, market checks and public campaigns reduce them; none ends them alone.
  • Inspectors can be bribed. Rotation, body cameras and published inspection results are the defense (Part 62).
  • Science changes. The banned list is reviewed every two years by the agency with independent scientists, and every change is explained publicly.

t: PART 107 — PAY THAT LETS PEOPLE LIVE WITH DIGNITY: A LIVING WAGE AND A SHARE OF THE PROFIT
h:
PART 107 — PAY THAT LETS PEOPLE LIVE WITH DIGNITY: A LIVING WAGE AND A SHARE OF THE PROFIT

107.1 The principle

A full-time job must pay enough to live with dignity: food, housing, transport, school for the children, health care, and a little saved. When a company makes a profit, the workers who made it receive a share.

107.2 The living wage

  1. A National Wage Council builds on Haiti's existing wage council: employers, unions, independent economists and citizens drawn by lot.
  2. The method is published: each year the council measures the cost of a basic basket for a family (food, rent, transport, school, health, clothing) in each département.
  3. The minimum wage is set from that cost and adjusted every year for prices. Sectors may have different minimums, never below the national floor.
  4. A path, not a jump: where today's wage is far below the living wage, the council sets a schedule to close the gap within a few years, so that jobs are not lost overnight.
  5. Paid always, paid on time, with a written contract (Part 74), through the payment rail (Part 32).

107.3 A share of the profit

Basing all pay on profits would be unfair to workers: profits change from year to year, can be hidden, and are often zero in a new company. So base pay is the living wage or more, always, and profit sharing comes on top:

  1. Every company with 20 or more workers shares a part of its net profit with its workers each year, by a formula set in law (for example, a fixed share of profit after tax). France has required this of companies with 50 or more employees for decades.
  2. Every worker receives a share, in proportion to salary and time worked, with a minimum for the lowest paid.
  3. The accounts are audited, and workers' representatives can see them. Hiding profit (for example by paying it out to related companies abroad) is fraud.
  4. The share is lightly taxed for the worker, and the company receives a tax allowance (Part 103.4).
  5. Smaller companies are encouraged to share profits voluntarily, with the same tax advantages.

107.4 Fair pay inside the company

  • Large companies publish the ratio between the highest salary and the middle salary.
  • Equal pay for women and men for the same work.
  • The public service follows the same grade system (Part 7), and pays the living wage at the lowest grade.

107.5 Honest limits

  • A minimum wage set too high, too fast, can push jobs into the informal sector or abroad, especially in clothing factories. That is why the council uses evidence and a schedule.
  • Most Haitians work for themselves. A wage law does not reach them; credit (Part 98), markets (Part 95) and the small-business tax (Part 103) do.
  • Profit sharing depends on honest accounts. Audits and penalties for hidden profits are the condition.

PART 108 — RECORD OF THIS REVISION (PARTS 103–107, AND CHANGES TO PARTS 98 AND 101)

108.1 What changed

Older text Change
Part 59: costing and growth A full tax system with low rates, a wide base, pay by phone, the receipt that shows the use, a 20% ceiling and a National Reserve Fund (Part 103)

Haitians receive the same sentences and cost orders, without deportation

108.2 What was checked, and what was not

Checked: Haiti's tax revenue (World Bank figures in a September 2025 press article); the 2023 Latin American and OECD averages (Inter-American Development Bank); Haiti's income tax brackets and 10% TCA (a tax guide); the 2012 disability law and its 2% quota (press article); the 2011 report of fewer than 20 psychiatrists (press article); the Minamata Convention's rule on mercury in cosmetics (Convention website); the delays of the US proposal to ban formaldehyde in hair straighteners (press reports).

Not verified: Haiti's current company tax rate and property tax rules; the current number of mental health professionals; the date Haiti ratified the disability convention and whether Haiti is a party to the Minamata Convention; the details of France's profit-sharing law; the current composition of Haiti's wage council.

108.3 Open decisions added

  1. The income tax rates, the company tax rate, and the 15% revenue target and 20% ceiling (Part 103).
  2. The share of revenue saved each year and the size of the National Reserve Fund (Part 103.8).
  3. The public-service disability quota of 4% (Part 104).
  4. The profit-sharing formula and the company size from which it applies (Part 107).
  5. The maximum extra detention for a foreigner who can pay the costs of Part 101.5 and refuses (Part 101.5).

t: SUMMARY: WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD
h:
SUMMARY: WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

This document is designed to be handed to a legislative drafting body, an economist, or any reviewer to continue refining — it is a structural skeleton, not a finished constitution. The next honest step for any part of it is the same question asked throughout: if this specific office or rule were captured or abused, what stops it — and is that stopping mechanism a different body, selected a different way, on a different timeline, than the thing it's checking? Wherever the answer is "nothing" or "the same people," that section needs another pass before implementation.

What the October 2026 revision (Parts 37–47) changed in the overall picture: the system now has a symbolic root (the 1805 Charter), an honest legal route (Part 38: ordinary law now, advisory citizen panels next, strict constitutional change last), a defense for the period between selection and swearing-in (Part 39), a child-protection framework that regulates fundraising appeals without regulating speech (Part 40), a judgment-first path out of armed groups (Part 41), prisons and a technology hub that give people a trade (Parts 42–43), a public force that no foreign party commands or pays (Part 44), a strict, origin-neutral trade gate plus a lawful cost for disrespect of Haitians anywhere (Part 45), a review that lists what cannot be fixed by design (Part 46), and a way for anyone to comment and vote on every section (Part 47).

What the November 2026 revision (Parts 48–60) changed: Haitian officials now have a duty to speak, with evidence, whenever Haitians are abused during deportation, while accepting every country's right to apply its immigration law (Part 48). The border is built as four borders: the Line, the Gates, the coast, and the ports and airports (Part 49). Food sold in Haiti must meet one high health standard that applies to every country and to Haitian producers alike (Part 50), and Haitian farmers are paid to meet it (Part 51). Haitians abroad are invited home, with the obstacles removed and no false promises (Part 52). Private guns end in stages and no service weapon goes home (Part 53). Identity and passports get one permanent, independent house (Part 54); every ministry and embassy shares one State Technology Center (Part 55); a counter-intelligence service protects the state without arrest powers and without watching citizens' politics (Part 56). Family, language, history and faith are protected without policing private life (Part 57). No office is left empty (Part 58). Nothing starts without a published cost sheet (Part 59).

What the second November 2026 revision (Parts 61–68) changed: private firearms are deposited by a fixed date and returned only through an examination stricter than Japan's (Part 61); blades and tools are not carried in public without a lawful reason (Part 62); racism is a crime tried in ordinary courts (Part 63); every new building needs a Certificate of Safety from licensed builders and independent inspectors, and families can borrow to build (Part 64); towns stay low, green and planned, schools host no concerts, and investors build licensed venues (Part 65); every household gets safe water (Part 66) and waste collection (Part 67); and the goal of being the safest country is measured each year on a public scorecard (Part 68).

What the third November 2026 revision (Parts 69–79) changed: deposited firearms stay their owners' property and every purchase needs its own permit; handguns are excluded (Part 69). Racial insult brings community work twice, then prison, with an Equality Unit in every département (Part 69). Water and waste are under public control (Part 69). A national cleanliness service, protected road-maintenance money and fast repair keep the country in order (Part 70). Waste becomes gas, materials and power, and companies take back their bottles (Part 71). Children learn first from books, paper and teachers (Part 72), and the State University is rebuilt as great campuses with research (Part 73). Every job has a written contract and wages are enforced within weeks (Part 74). Wealth is opened to the majority by access, not by seizure (Part 75). Young people used by armed groups who committed no grave crime get a supervised way back (Part 76). History's great crimes get an official public truth, and living suspects face permanent chambers of the ordinary courts (Part 77). One existing city is renewed as the model for the rest (Part 78).

What the fourth November 2026 revision (Parts 80–89) changed: the Executive Council keeps seven members but gains what earlier councils lacked: members chosen one by one, nothing to share out, a majority rule with a deadline, one First Coordinator for two years, and public votes (Part 80). Each commune has one Mayor and each section one Coordinator (Part 81). Council members are born in Haiti and at least 35; the diaspora may serve elsewhere; those who govern live in Haiti with their families (Part 82). Lawyers and every profession enter by national examination and answer to independent discipline (Part 83). The transfer levy and PetroCaribe are audited in full, and no levy exists without a public ledger (Part 84). Restavèk and street childhood end by a set date (Part 85). Energy has an independent referee (Part 86). Embassies are audited before they are changed (Part 87). The work is protected by copyright and downloads are recorded (Part 88). The border Line is staffed day and night, and border markets run under published rules (Part 90).

What the fifth November 2026 revision (Parts 91–97) changed: no salary is paid to anyone hired outside a published ranked list, and every ministry's hiring belongs to one independent human-resources house (Part 91). Citizens may aim for a skilled role through a targeted pool, by exam and qualification, never by paying for better odds (Part 91.5). Every public worker swears to serve the country, not a party, and every office posts what it needs, what it costs and how long it takes (Part 92). The Assembly meets on a fixed calendar, votes by name, and fills any empty seat from a reserve list within two weeks (Part 93). Every official is trained before serving, including how to defend Haiti abroad (Part 94). Each commune's food is mapped and moved by a cool chain and coastal boats (Part 95). Every school gets a field, a court and a PE teacher, with championships from the commune to the nation (Part 96).

What the sixth November 2026 revision (Parts 98–102) changed: every adult gets a free account, and farmers and small firms can borrow against animals, tools, contracts and stored harvests, with a guarantee fund, index insurance and one clear price in Kreyòl (Part 98). The konbit, mutual help at birth and death, the lakou and community mediation are protected, and services and agencies move out of the crowded capital (Part 99). Haitian music and stories get airtime and money, children are protected by age, time and place, and only a judge can ban content that recruits for armed groups, threatens, or celebrates real crimes (Part 100). Drugs are illegal to make, sell, carry or use; traffickers lose their assets; first-time users choose treatment or prison; foreign offenders pay the costs of their case, are deported, and are banned for at least five years (Parts 101, 108).

What the seventh November 2026 revision (Parts 103–108) changed: taxes stay light (never above 20% of GDP without a two-thirds vote), few and simple, paid by phone, with no income tax on the living wage and a receipt that shows where the money went; 3% of revenue each year goes to a National Reserve Fund for disasters (Part 103). The 2012 disability law is enforced, with inclusive schools, sign language, access and work quotas (Part 104). Mental health care reaches every section and commune, with a 24-hour line and no chains (Part 105). Buyers get refunds, labels and fast small claims, and mercury, cosmetic hydroquinone, formaldehyde straighteners and skin-lightening advertising are banned (Part 106). Pay is at least a living wage, and companies of 20 or more share profits with workers (Part 107).
